title: Irish brown soda bread
skill: A quick bread mixed only until it comes together

move.title: Quick hands, a deep cross
move.body: Brown soda bread is the everyday loaf of Irish home kitchens: whole-wheat flour, oats, and buttermilk, raised with baking soda instead of yeast. Today you'll weigh the flours, stir in the buttermilk only until there are no dry patches, shape the soft dough in a few seconds, and cut a deep cross in the top before it bakes to 200°F.

callback.body: Cornbread's batter rose from buttermilk and baking soda. Soda bread uses the same pair, in a dough thick enough to shape by hand. Just as with the cornbread, the less you mix it, the lighter it bakes.

why.title: Soda and buttermilk
why.body: Baking soda makes its bubbles as soon as it meets the acid in buttermilk. The gas only lasts so long, so the dough is shaped and in the oven within a few minutes of mixing.

why.title: Why weigh the flour
why.body: Whole-wheat flour packs down in a cup more than white flour does, so a scooped cup can be far too much. Too much flour makes the loaf heavy and dry. The scale gives the same loaf every time.

why.title: Quick, light hands
why.body: Stirring and kneading build gluten, which makes a quick bread tough and dense. Mix just until there's no dry flour, and shape it with a few gentle turns, not a knead.

why.title: The deep cross
why.body: A thick round loaf bakes slowly in the middle. Cutting a cross halfway down opens the center to the heat, so it bakes through before the crust gets too dark. It also lets the loaf split where you want it to.

why.title: 200°F, and a hollow knock
why.body: A soda bread is baked through when its center reads 200°F. Tap the bottom too: a done loaf sounds hollow.

wrong.sign: The loaf spread flat on the pan
wrong.fix: The dough was too wet. Next time, hold back the last ¼ cup of buttermilk and add it only if there are dry patches.
It was mixed or handled too much, or the flour was scooped. Weigh the flour and stop stirring as soon as it comes together.

wrong.sign: There are yellow-green specks and a bitter taste
wrong.fix: Lumps of baking soda. Press it through your fingers into the flour and whisk well before the buttermilk goes in.

wrong.sign: The crust is dark but the center reads under 200°F
wrong.fix: Lay foil loosely over the top and bake 5 more minutes.

quiz.q: Why does the dough go in the oven right after mixing?
choices: The soda's bubbles start as soon as it meets the buttermilk
quiz.explain: Wait too long and the gas escapes before the bread sets.

quiz.q: Why cut a deep cross in the top?
choices: It opens the thick center to the heat so it bakes through
quiz.explain: It also controls where the loaf splits.

quiz.q: How do you know a soda bread is done?
choices: 200°F in the center, and a hollow sound from the bottom
When the top is dark brown

substitutions.note: Stir 2 tablespoons of oil into the buttermilk instead of rubbing butter into the flour.

steps.text: Put a rack in the middle of the oven and heat it to 425°F. Line the sheet pan with parchment.
Set the large bowl on the scale and zero it. Weigh in 8.5 ounces of whole-wheat flour, zero it, and weigh in 4.4 ounces of all-purpose flour.
steps.tip: No scale? Spoon the flour into the cup and level it with the back of a knife. Don't pack it.

steps.text: Add the oats, brown sugar, and salt. Rub the baking soda between your fingers over the bowl to break up any lumps, then whisk everything for 30 seconds.
Add the cold butter cubes and rub them into the flour with your fingertips until no lumps of butter are left.
steps.look: Like coarse sand, with no butter showing.

steps.text: Make a hollow in the middle and pour in 1½ cups of the buttermilk. Stir with the fork in wide circles, from the middle out, just until there are no dry patches. Add the last ¼ cup only if it's still dry at the bottom.
steps.look: A soft, sticky, shaggy dough with no dry flour.
steps.tip: Don't taste the raw dough. Raw flour can make you sick.

steps.text: Dust the counter with flour and tip the dough out. With floured hands, tuck the edges under two or three times to make a round, then pat it to about 2 inches high and 7 inches across. Lift it onto the pan.
steps.tip: Ten seconds of handling is plenty. It doesn't need to be smooth.

steps.text: Dip the knife in flour and cut a deep cross across the whole top, halfway down through the loaf, from edge to edge.
Turn the oven down to 400°F and bake until the loaf is deep brown and the cross has opened.
steps.look: Deep brown, and the cross has opened wide.

steps.text: With oven mitts, take out the pan. Push the thermometer into the center from the side: 200°F. Tip the loaf up with a mitt and tap the bottom: it should sound hollow. If either check fails, bake 5 more minutes and check again.
Turn off the oven. Wrap the loaf in the towel on the cooling rack for a soft crust, or leave it bare for a crisp one, and let it cool before slicing.
steps.tip: It's best the day it's baked. Slice and freeze what's left.
